newsitem.title: USA: GE jet engine deal seen boosting earnings.
newsitem.headline: GE jet engine deal seen boosting earnings.

text.p: General Electric Co.'s agreement to acquire Greenwich Air Services Inc and UNC Inc will eventually boost GE's earnings because servicing aircraft engines is more profitable than manufacturing them, analysts said on Monday.
The $875 million deal also gives GE a competitive advantage and allows it to extend its engine services business into a new market segment -- business jets, analysts said.

"The reason this deal was done was that it got GE into a new category segment -- business jets," said Nick Heymann, analyst at NatWest Securities. "You now have GE really very strong in virtually all facets of the aircraft engine business."
Heymann said the acquisition would be "slightly additive" to GE's earnings by the second half of this year. "It will be meaningfully additive, several cents a share, next year."
GE stock was up 0-1/2 to 105-7/8 on volume of 1.4 million shares at 1445 EST.
GE has said for some time that it views a company-wide expansion into the services area as a major driver of growth in the 21st century.
Engine maintenance enjoys a higher return on investment than engine manufacturing, said Bill Fiala, an analyst at Edward Jones in St. Louis.
"They've been very aggressive in the pricing of their aircraft engines, which has driven down the profitability," Fiala said. "They do see a higher return on investment in the service side of it."

The acquisition will also give GE a competitive edge. "GE can not only provide the engines, but when it comes to making a sales call, they also can deliver on world-class service, and it's going to help them more often than not in making the sale," Fiala said.
"I think that this transaction over time will help the profitability of GE's aircraft engine sales," added Wolfgang Demisch, managing director of BT Securities.
Heymann said the worldwide aircraft engine service and maintenance business is about $18-20 billion annually. The acquisition should give GE a 25-30 percent share of this market, he said.
One Wall Street analyst said the acqusition came as a slight surprise, since Greenwich Air Services was already in the process of acquiring UNC Inc.
"I'm a little surprised (GE) had to wait until someone bid up the price of UNC, when Greenwich made a bid for that," she said.

It was also surprising because an aviation trade press report had recently speculated that United Technologies Corp unit Pratt & Whitney was a possible buyer of Greenwich once the UNC deal was completed, she said.

For GE, the acquisition was "all about taking an advantage they have, which is knowing about aircraft engines, and trying to put that in a marketplace where the margins are higher, because the original equipment aircraft engine market has become so competitive," the Wall Street analyst said.
GE Engine Services, a wholly owned subsidiary of GE that is based in Evendale, Ohio, had revenues of approximately $2.3 billion in 1996. ((--Matthew Lewis, Hartford newsroom (860) 727-0224))
